items.body: In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent set of rules rich enough to describe arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. No single list of axioms can capture all of mathematics.

items.title: The Riemann hypothesis
items.body: Proposed in 1859, it predicts where the zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie, which governs how prime numbers are spread out. It is a Millennium Prize Problem with a 1 million dollar reward, and it remains unsolved.

items.title: The four colour theorem
items.body: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so that no neighbouring regions match. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved it in 1976, the first major theorem proved with heavy help from a computer.

items.title: Derivative check
items.body: Calculus check.
items.statement: The derivative of x³ is 3x²
items.explanation: Power rule: the derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹, so x³ becomes 3x².

items.title: Integral check
items.body: Calculus check.
items.statement: The integral of 2x is x² + C
items.explanation: The derivative of x² is 2x, so integrating 2x gives x² plus a constant of integration C.

items.title: Is √2 a fraction?
items.body: Number theory check.
items.statement: √2 can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers
items.explanation: Assuming √2 = p/q in lowest terms forces both p and q to be even, a contradiction.

items.title: 0.999... and 1
items.body: Real numbers check.
items.statement: 0.999... (repeating forever) equals exactly 1
items.explanation: Let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999..., so 10x − x = 9, giving 9x = 9 and x = 1.

items.title: A logarithm
items.body: Logarithms check.
items.explanation: 10³ = 1000, so the base-10 logarithm of 1000 is 3.

items.title: A trig identity
items.body: Trigonometry check.
items.statement: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle θ
items.explanation: It is Pythagoras' theorem on a circle of radius 1: the sides are cos θ and sin θ, the hypotenuse is 1.

items.title: Euler's identity check
items.body: Complex numbers check.
items.explanation: By Euler's formula, e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1, so adding 1 gives 0.

items.title: Reading a blood pressure
items.body: Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120/80 mmHg. The top (systolic) is the pressure as the heart squeezes; the bottom (diastolic) is between beats. The WHO defines hypertension as 140/90 or higher on repeated readings. It usually has no symptoms.

items.title: Resting heart rate
items.body: A normal adult resting heart rate is about 60 to 100 beats per minute. Fit athletes can be in the 40s because each beat pumps more blood. A fast resting rate can come from fever, dehydration, anaemia, stress, caffeine or heart problems.

items.title: What blood is made of
items.body: Blood is about 55% plasma (water, salts, proteins, sugar) and 45% cells. Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; white cells fight infection; platelets start clotting. Anaemia means too little haemoglobin, causing tiredness and breathlessness.

items.title: Blood groups
items.body: Red cells carry A, B, both or neither antigen (groups A, B, AB, O), plus Rh positive or negative. The wrong transfusion triggers a dangerous immune reaction. O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone in an emergency; AB positive patients can receive any group.

items.title: How vaccines work
items.body: A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ. It learns to recognise it and keeps memory cells, so a later real infection is fought off fast, often before you get sick. Vaccines have eliminated smallpox and nearly eliminated polio.

items.title: Viruses versus bacteria
items.body: Bacteria are living cells; many are harmless or helpful. Viruses are far smaller and can only multiply inside our cells. Antibiotics kill bacteria but do nothing to viruses, so they don't help colds or flu. Some viruses have antivirals, such as ART for HIV.

items.title: Malaria
items.body: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Fever, chills and headache after travel to a malaria area need a rapid diagnostic test the same day. It is curable with artemisinin-based combination therapy, but severe malaria can kill within a day.

items.title: HIV and antiretroviral therapy
items.body: HIV attacks CD4 immune cells. Daily antiretroviral therapy (ART) stops the virus multiplying, lets the immune system recover and gives a near-normal life expectancy. A person whose viral load stays undetectable on ART does not pass HIV to sexual partners.
items.source_name: World Health Organization: HIV and AIDS

items.title: Tuberculosis is curable
items.body: TB is a bacterial infection spread through the air, usually affecting the lungs. Warning signs: a cough for over two weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Standard treatment is a combination of antibiotics for about six months, and finishing the course prevents drug-resistant TB.

items.title: Cholera and oral rehydration
items.body: Cholera spreads through water or food contaminated with faeces and causes severe watery diarrhoea. Most patients can be saved with oral rehydration solution (ORS) given quickly. Safe water, sanitation and hand washing prevent outbreaks.

items.title: Type 2 diabetes
items.body: In type 2 diabetes the body stops responding well to insulin, so blood sugar stays high and slowly damages eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels. Risk rises with excess weight and inactivity. Diet, exercise and medicines such as metformin control it.

items.title: Body mass index
items.body: BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in m)². 18.5–24.9 counts as a healthy range for most adults, 25–29.9 overweight and 30+ obese. It is a quick screening tool, not a diagnosis: very muscular people score high, and waist size adds useful information.

items.title: Spot a stroke: FAST
items.body: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty: Time to get emergency help. A stroke is a blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain, and about two million brain cells die each minute it is untreated. Clot-busting treatment works only in the first few hours.

items.title: Heart attack warning signs
items.body: A heart attack is a blocked artery starving heart muscle of oxygen. Typical signs: crushing chest pain or pressure lasting minutes, spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Women and diabetics may have milder symptoms. Get help immediately.

items.title: Hands-only CPR
items.body: If an adult collapses and is not breathing normally, call for help and push hard and fast in the centre of the chest: 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 times a minute, letting the chest rise fully. Use an AED as soon as one arrives. Doing something is far better than nothing.

items.title: Drug half-life
items.body: Half-life is the time for a drug's blood level to halve. After four to five half-lives it is mostly gone, and with regular doses it reaches a steady state in about the same time. That is why some medicines take days to work fully.

items.title: Antibiotic resistance
items.body: When antibiotics are overused or courses stopped early, surviving bacteria that resist the drug multiply. The WHO ranks antimicrobial resistance among the top global health threats. Use antibiotics only when prescribed and take the full course as directed.

items.title: Why sleep matters
items.body: During sleep the brain consolidates memories and clears waste products. Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours. Regular short sleep is linked to poorer concentration, weaker immunity, weight gain, high blood pressure and more accidents, including at the wheel.

items.title: Paracetamol has a limit
items.body: Paracetamol is safe at normal doses, but too much damages the liver, sometimes fatally, and symptoms can take a day to appear. For adults the usual maximum is 4 g in 24 hours. Many cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol, so doses can add up by accident.

items.title: Randomised controlled trials
items.body: To test a treatment fairly, patients are randomly split into groups receiving the new treatment or a placebo or standard care. Double-blinding hides who gets what from both patients and doctors. Randomisation removes bias; blinding removes the effect of expectations.

items.title: Sensitivity and specificity
items.body: Sensitivity is the share of sick people a test correctly flags; specificity is the share of healthy people it correctly clears. When a disease is rare, even a 99% specific test produces many false positives, which is why positive screening results are confirmed.

items.title: The ECG
items.body: An electrocardiogram records the heart's electrical activity through skin electrodes. The P wave is the atria contracting, the QRS complex the ventricles, and the T wave their recovery. Irregular rhythms and heart attacks leave recognisable patterns.

items.title: Seeing inside the body
items.body: X-rays show bone well. CT combines many X-rays into 3D slices. MRI uses strong magnets and radio waves, with no ionising radiation, and shows soft tissue in detail. Ultrasound uses sound echoes, is cheap and safe, and is used in pregnancy.

items.title: Depression is treatable
items.body: Depression is more than sadness: low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks, often with poor sleep, low energy and hopelessness. It is common and treatable with talking therapies, and sometimes medicine. Anyone thinking of self-harm should seek help urgently.

items.title: About 100,000 heartbeats a day
items.body: At around 70 beats per minute, your heart beats about 100,000 times a day and about 2.5 billion times in a lifetime, pumping roughly 5 litres of blood every minute at rest.

items.title: Penicillin was found by accident
items.body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mould growing on a forgotten bacterial culture had killed the bacteria around it. Mass production during the 1940s turned penicillin into the first widely used antibiotic, saving millions of lives.

items.title: Antibiotics and flu
items.body: Infection check.
items.statement: Antibiotics cure the flu
items.explanation: Antibiotics only kill bacteria. Flu is caused by a virus; rest, fluids and sometimes antivirals help, and the flu vaccine prevents it.

items.title: High blood pressure
items.body: Cardiology check.
items.statement: A repeated reading of 140/90 mmHg counts as high blood pressure
items.explanation: The WHO defines hypertension as 140/90 mmHg or higher on repeated readings.

items.title: The universal donor
items.body: Blood check.
items.statement: O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone
items.explanation: O negative red cells carry no A, B or RhD antigens, so they are used in emergencies before the patient's group is known.

items.title: How malaria spreads
items.body: Infection check.
items.statement: Malaria spreads from person to person by coughing
items.explanation: Malaria parasites are carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Nets, repellents and indoor spraying prevent it.

items.title: Half-lives
items.body: Pharmacology check.
items.statement: After three half-lives, 12.5% of a drug remains
items.explanation: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5%. Each half-life halves what is left.

items.title: Separation of powers
items.body: Many constitutions split government into three branches: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them. The idea, linked to the French thinker Montesquieu, is that each branch checks the others.

items.title: Where 'democracy' comes from
items.body: The word democracy comes from the Greek 'demos' (people) and 'kratos' (power or rule): rule by the people. Ancient Athens practised an early direct form of it in the 5th century BCE.

items.title: Parliamentary systems
items.body: In a parliamentary system the head of government (usually a prime minister) comes from and depends on the support of parliament. If parliament loses confidence in the government, it can be removed. Examples include the UK, India and Japan.

items.title: Presidential systems
items.body: In a presidential system the president is both head of state and head of government, is elected separately from the legislature, and serves a fixed term. Examples include the United States, Brazil and Kenya.

items.title: What is federalism?
items.body: In a federal system, power is shared between a national government and regional governments such as states or provinces, each with its own powers set by the constitution. Examples: the United States, Nigeria, India and Germany.

items.title: What is a unitary state?
items.body: In a unitary state the central government holds most power. Local governments exist, but their powers are given, and can be changed, by the centre. France and Japan are examples.

items.title: What a constitution does
items.body: A constitution is the supreme law of a country. It sets out how government is organised, what powers each part has, and often the rights of citizens. Other laws must not contradict it.

items.title: Magna Carta, 1215
items.body: In 1215 King John of England agreed to Magna Carta, a charter limiting royal power. Its principle that even the ruler is subject to the law influenced later constitutions around the world.

items.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
items.body: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948. It sets out 30 articles of basic rights. 10 December is now Human Rights Day.
items.source_name: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

items.title: First past the post
items.body: Under 'first past the post', each area elects one representative: whoever gets the most votes wins, even without a majority. It is simple, but a party's share of seats can differ a lot from its share of votes.

items.title: Proportional representation
items.body: In proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in line with their share of the vote. 30% of votes gives about 30% of seats. It often leads to coalition governments. South Africa and the Netherlands use forms of it.

items.title: What is a referendum?
items.body: A referendum is a direct vote in which all voters decide on a single question, such as a new constitution or leaving an organisation, instead of leaving the decision to elected representatives.

items.title: Constitutional monarchy
items.body: In a constitutional monarchy, a king or queen is head of state but their powers are limited by a constitution, and elected politicians run the government. Examples: the UK, Japan and Lesotho. In an absolute monarchy, the monarch holds full power.

items.title: Two chambers
items.body: A bicameral legislature has two chambers, such as a lower house and an upper house or senate. Laws usually need approval from both. A unicameral legislature has only one chamber.

items.title: The rule of law
items.body: The rule of law means everyone, including government leaders, is subject to laws that are public, applied equally and decided by independent courts, rather than to the arbitrary will of those in power.

items.title: South Africa's 1994 election
items.body: South Africa's first election in which all races could vote was held in April 1994. Nelson Mandela became the country's first democratically elected president in May 1994.

items.title: The Berlin Wall falls
items.body: The Berlin Wall, which divided East and West Berlin from 1961, was opened on 9 November 1989. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.

items.title: Women's right to vote
items.body: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all women the right to vote in national elections.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Women's suffrage in New Zealand

items.title: What is impeachment?
items.body: Impeachment is a process in which a legislature formally charges a senior official, such as a president, with serious misconduct. Depending on the country, a conviction can lead to removal from office.

items.title: Coalition governments
items.body: When no single party wins a majority, two or more parties may agree to govern together as a coalition, sharing ministries and agreeing a common programme.

items.title: Judicial review
items.body: Judicial review is the power of courts to check whether laws or government actions follow the constitution, and to strike them down if they do not.

items.title: Head of state vs head of government
items.body: The head of state represents the country, often in a ceremonial role. The head of government runs the government day to day. In some countries one person does both; in others, like Germany, they are separate.

items.title: Why 'left' and 'right'?
items.body: The terms left and right in politics come from the French Revolution. In the National Assembly of 1789, supporters of the king sat on the right of the president and supporters of revolution on the left.

items.title: Term limits
items.body: A term limit restricts how many times, or how long, a person can hold an office. Many presidential systems limit presidents to two terms. Supporters see them as a check on power; critics say voters should decide.

items.title: Ghana's independence, 1957
items.body: Ghana, formerly the Gold Coast, gained independence from Britain on 6 March 1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah. It was among the first colonies in sub-Saharan Africa to become independent.

items.title: The role of the opposition
items.body: Parties not in government form the opposition. They question and scrutinise the government, propose alternative policies and offer voters a choice at the next election.

items.title: Politics word: sovereignty
items.body: Meaning: supreme authority of a state to govern itself without outside interference.
items.example_sentence: The treaty respects each country's sovereignty over its own borders.

items.title: Politics word: manifesto
items.body: Meaning: a public statement of a party's policies and aims, usually published before an election.
items.example_sentence: The party's manifesto promised free school meals.

items.title: Politics word: constituency
items.body: Meaning: an area whose voters elect a representative, and also the voters themselves.
items.example_sentence: She held regular meetings with people in her constituency.

items.title: Politics word: veto
items.body: Meaning: the power to reject a decision or law. From Latin for 'I forbid'.
items.example_sentence: The president used a veto to block the bill.

items.title: Politics word: incumbent
items.body: Meaning: the person who currently holds an office.
items.example_sentence: The incumbent mayor is running for a second term.

items.title: Politics word: electorate
items.body: Meaning: all the people entitled to vote in an election.
items.example_sentence: Young people make up a growing share of the electorate.

items.title: Where prime ministers come from
items.body: Systems of government.
items.statement: In a parliamentary system, the head of government usually comes from the legislature
items.explanation: The prime minister is usually a member of parliament and needs its support to stay in office.

items.title: Who makes laws?
items.body: Branches of government.
items.statement: The judiciary's main role is to make laws
items.explanation: The legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out and the judiciary interprets and applies them.

items.title: Magna Carta date
items.body: History check.
items.statement: Magna Carta was agreed in 1815
items.explanation: King John agreed to Magna Carta in 1215, six centuries earlier.

items.title: Direct democracy
items.body: Voting check.
items.statement: A referendum lets citizens vote directly on a specific question
items.explanation: In a referendum voters decide one question themselves instead of leaving it to representatives.

items.title: Human rights declaration
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948
items.explanation: The UN General Assembly adopted it on 10 December 1948 in Paris.
items.source_name: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

items.title: Federal power
items.body: Systems of government.
items.statement: In a federal system, all power belongs to the central government
items.explanation: Federal systems share power between national and regional governments. Central control describes a unitary state.

items.title: Mandela's presidency
items.body: History check.
items.statement: Nelson Mandela became president of South Africa in 1994
items.explanation: He was inaugurated in May 1994 after the country's first fully democratic election.

items.title: The Berlin Wall
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The Berlin Wall fell in 1991
items.explanation: The wall was opened on 9 November 1989. German reunification followed in 1990.

items.title: Counting chambers
items.body: Parliament check.
items.statement: A 'bicameral' parliament has two chambers
items.explanation: 'Bi' means two. A bicameral parliament has two houses, such as an assembly and a senate.

items.title: Duverger's law
items.body: Political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two dominant parties, because voters desert small parties that cannot win seats. Proportional representation tends to support many parties.

items.title: The median voter theorem
items.body: In a two-party race on a single issue, parties are pulled towards the position of the median voter, so their platforms converge. It helps explain why big parties can sound alike close to an election.

items.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
items.body: In 1951 economist Kenneth Arrow proved that no ranked voting system with three or more options can meet a short list of reasonable fairness conditions all at once. Every electoral system involves trade-offs.

items.title: Presidential term limits in Zimbabwe
items.body: Under the 2013 Constitution, a person may serve as President for at most two five-year terms. Term limits exist to prevent power becoming personal and to guarantee regular, peaceful handovers.

items.title: The birth of the United Nations
items.body: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945, now celebrated as United Nations Day. The UN replaced the League of Nations, created after World War I.

items.title: The UN Security Council
items.body: The Security Council has 15 members. Five are permanent and hold a veto: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The other ten are elected for two-year terms.

items.title: 193 member states
items.body: As of 2025, the United Nations has 193 member states. South Sudan, in 2011, was the most recent country to join. Two observer states, the Holy See and Palestine, are not full members.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Member states of the United Nations

items.title: The African Union
items.body: The African Union (AU) was launched in 2002 in Durban, South Africa, replacing the Organisation of African Unity. It has 55 member states and its headquarters are in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

items.title: Africa Day
items.body: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 independent African states. 25 May is celebrated as Africa Day.

items.title: SADC
items.body: The Southern African Development Community (SADC) promotes economic integration, peace and security in southern Africa. It was established in 1992, succeeding a coordination conference formed in 1980. Its headquarters are in Gaborone, Botswana.

items.title: ECOWAS
items.body: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was founded by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975 to promote economic integration in West Africa. Its headquarters are in Abuja, Nigeria.

items.title: The European Union
items.body: The European Union is a political and economic union of European countries. As of 2025 it has 27 member states, after the United Kingdom left in 2020. Most members use the euro as their currency.

items.title: NATO
items.body: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is a military alliance founded in 1949. Under Article 5 of its treaty, an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

items.title: Embassies and consulates
items.body: An embassy is a country's main diplomatic mission in a foreign capital, led by an ambassador. Consulates are smaller offices, often in other cities, that help citizens abroad and issue visas.

items.title: Diplomatic immunity
items.body: The 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations sets the rules for diplomacy, including diplomatic immunity: diplomats cannot be prosecuted by the host country, though they can be expelled.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations

items.title: The Peace of Westphalia
items.body: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe. It is often seen as the origin of the modern idea of sovereign states that do not interfere in each other's internal affairs.

items.title: Bretton Woods, 1944
items.body: At the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire, USA, in July 1944, 44 Allied nations agreed a new international monetary system and created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

items.title: The World Trade Organization
items.body: The World Trade Organization (WTO) began on 1 January 1995, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947. It sets rules for trade between nations and settles trade disputes. It is based in Geneva.

items.title: BRICS
items.body: BRICS began as a grouping of Brazil, Russia, India and China; South Africa joined in 2010. The group expanded from 2024 with new members including Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

items.title: The Non-Aligned Movement
items.body: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in Belgrade in 1961 by countries that chose not to formally join either side in the Cold War. Leaders of India, Egypt, Yugoslavia, Ghana and Indonesia played key roles.

items.title: Hard power and soft power
items.body: Hard power is getting what you want through force or payment, like military action or sanctions. Soft power, a term coined by Joseph Nye, is attraction: culture, values and policies that make others want to cooperate.

items.title: The Commonwealth
items.body: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of 56 member countries, as of 2025, most of them former British territories. Gabon and Togo, which have no historic ties to Britain, joined in 2022.

items.title: The International Court of Justice
items.body: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), in The Hague, Netherlands, is the UN's main court. It settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms.

items.title: The International Criminal Court
items.body: The International Criminal Court (ICC), which began work in 2002 in The Hague, tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. Unlike the ICJ, it prosecutes people, not states.

items.title: Economic sanctions
items.body: Sanctions are penalties one or more countries place on another, such as trade bans, frozen assets or travel bans, to pressure a change in behaviour without using military force.

items.title: The Geneva Conventions
items.body: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 set rules for the humane treatment of wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and civilians during armed conflict. Every UN member state has ratified them.

items.title: The Paris Agreement
items.body: Adopted in December 2015, the Paris Agreement on climate change aims to keep global warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

items.title: The UN General Assembly
items.body: The General Assembly is the UN body where all 193 member states meet, each with one vote regardless of size. Its resolutions are mostly recommendations; binding decisions on peace and security come from the Security Council.

items.title: Bilateral and multilateral
items.body: Bilateral relations are between two countries, such as a trade deal between Kenya and India. Multilateral relations involve three or more countries, often through organisations such as the UN, the AU or the WTO.

items.title: Word: ratify
items.body: Meaning: to formally approve a treaty so it becomes legally binding on a country, usually through parliament.
items.example_sentence: Parliament voted to ratify the trade agreement.

items.title: Word: embargo
items.body: Meaning: an official ban on trade or other activity with a particular country.
items.example_sentence: The arms embargo banned all weapons sales to the region.

items.title: Word: envoy
items.body: Meaning: a messenger or representative sent by a government on a special diplomatic mission.
items.example_sentence: The UN sent a special envoy to help with peace talks.

items.title: Word: détente
items.body: Meaning: the easing of tension between rival countries. Often used for the Cold War period of the 1970s.
items.example_sentence: The summit marked a new détente between the two neighbours.

items.title: Word: bloc
items.body: Meaning: a group of countries that act together because of shared interests.
items.example_sentence: The trade bloc negotiated as one with larger economies.

items.title: Veto powers
items.body: UN check.
items.statement: The UN Security Council has five permanent members with a veto
items.explanation: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US can each veto Security Council resolutions.

items.title: AU headquarters
items.body: Africa check.
items.statement: The African Union's headquarters is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
items.explanation: The AU, like the OAU before it, is based in Addis Ababa.

items.title: SADC headquarters
items.body: Africa check.
items.statement: SADC's headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya
items.explanation: SADC is based in Gaborone. Kenya is not a SADC member; it belongs to the East African Community.

items.title: When the UN began
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The United Nations was founded in 1919
items.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 after World War II. The League of Nations came first, after World War I.

items.title: NATO's founding
items.body: History check.
items.statement: NATO was founded in 1949
items.explanation: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington in April 1949.

items.title: The World Court
items.body: International law check.
items.statement: The International Court of Justice is in The Hague
items.explanation: The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague.

items.title: Why 25 May?
items.body: Africa check.
items.statement: Africa Day on 25 May marks the founding of the OAU in 1963
items.explanation: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963.

items.title: From GATT to WTO
items.body: Trade check.
items.statement: The WTO replaced GATT in 1995
items.explanation: The WTO started on 1 January 1995 and took over the GATT rules.

items.title: Votes in the General Assembly
items.body: UN check.
items.statement: Every UN member state has one vote in the General Assembly
items.explanation: Each of the 193 members has one vote, whatever its size or wealth.

items.title: Bretton Woods
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The IMF and World Bank were created at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944
items.explanation: 44 Allied nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944 and created both institutions.

items.title: The security dilemma
items.body: When one state arms to feel safe, its neighbours feel less safe and arm too. Both end up spending more and feeling less secure, even if neither wanted conflict. It is a central idea in realist theory.

items.title: Democratic peace theory
items.body: Established democracies have very rarely, if ever, fought wars against each other. Suggested reasons include accountable leaders, shared norms and trade ties, though scholars still debate the causes and the definitions.

items.title: The Thucydides trap
items.body: Political scientist Graham Allison argues that when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, war becomes more likely, as with Athens and Sparta. The idea is often applied to US–China rivalry, and is also widely criticised.

items.title: The Responsibility to Protect
items.body: Endorsed by all UN members in 2005, R2P says states must protect their people from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, and others may act if they fail. The 2011 Libya intervention made it controversial.

items.title: Sunlight is 8 minutes old
items.body: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. When you look at the Sun, you see it as it was just over 8 minutes ago.

items.title: Boiling point and altitude
items.body: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level. Higher up, air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature. On top of Mount Everest it boils at roughly 70 °C, which is why cooking takes longer there.

items.title: 206 bones
items.body: An adult human skeleton usually has 206 bones. Babies are born with around 270, and many of them fuse together as the body grows.

items.title: The double helix
items.body: In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described DNA's double helix structure. Their model relied on X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling.

items.title: How photosynthesis works
items.body: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose (sugar) and oxygen. It happens mainly in the leaves, inside chloroplasts, using the green pigment chlorophyll. Almost all oxygen we breathe comes from it.

items.title: The speed of light
items.body: Light travels through a vacuum at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, about 300,000 km every second. Nothing carrying information can travel faster.

items.title: What causes tides
items.body: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans, with a smaller effect from the Sun. Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides a day.

items.title: The biggest planet
items.body: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. It is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined, and about 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

items.title: The hottest planet
items.body: Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping the surface around 465 °C, hot enough to melt lead.

items.title: Antibiotics and viruses
items.body: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing. They do not work against viruses such as colds and flu. Using them when they are not needed helps bacteria become resistant.

items.title: The discovery of penicillin
items.body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould, Penicillium, killed bacteria growing in a dish in his London lab. Penicillin became the first widely used antibiotic in the 1940s.

items.title: Why blood is red
items.body: Red blood cells are full of haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body. The iron-based haem group gives blood its red colour.

items.title: The speed of sound
items.body: Sound travels through air at about 343 metres per second at 20 °C. It moves faster through water and even faster through solids like steel.

items.title: 118 elements
items.body: The periodic table has 118 confirmed chemical elements. The last four, including oganesson (element 118), were officially named in 2016.

items.title: Diamond and graphite
items.body: Diamond and graphite (the 'lead' in pencils) are both pure carbon. The only difference is how the carbon atoms are arranged, which makes one the hardest natural material and the other soft.

items.title: What air is made of
items.body: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and nearly 1% argon. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%, but it has a big effect on the climate.

items.title: 86 billion neurons
items.body: The human brain contains roughly 86 billion nerve cells (neurons), connected by trillions of synapses. It uses about 20% of the body's energy while making up only about 2% of body weight.

items.title: How vaccines work
items.body: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise a germ, using a harmless part or weakened form of it. If the real germ arrives later, the body can fight it faster.

items.title: The cell's power plants
items.body: Mitochondria produce most of the chemical energy a cell uses, in the form of a molecule called ATP. They have their own small set of DNA, inherited from the mother.

items.title: Around Earth in 90 minutes
items.body: The International Space Station travels at about 28,000 km/h and circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes, so astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises a day.

items.title: Moore's law
items.body: In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years. This trend drove decades of faster, cheaper computers.

items.title: Absolute zero
items.body: Absolute zero, −273.15 °C (0 kelvin), is the lowest possible temperature, where particles have the least possible energy. Scientists have cooled matter to within billionths of a degree of it.

items.title: Newton's first law
items.body: An object stays still, or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force acts on it. This is inertia. It is why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

items.title: A light-year is a distance
items.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion km. It measures distance, not time. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

items.title: Inside an atom
items.body: An atom has a tiny nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by electrons (negative). The number of protons decides which element it is: 6 protons is always carbon.

items.title: The pH scale
items.body: pH measures how acidic or alkaline a liquid is, usually from 0 to 14. 7 is neutral (pure water). Below 7 is acidic, like lemon juice; above 7 is alkaline, like soap.

items.title: The greenhouse effect
items.body: Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour let sunlight in but trap some of the heat Earth gives off. Without it, Earth would be far too cold for life; more of these gases warm the planet further.

items.title: Science word: catalyst
items.body: Meaning: a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. Enzymes are catalysts in living things.
items.example_sentence: Enzymes in saliva act as a catalyst to break down starch.

items.title: Science word: osmosis
items.body: Meaning: the movement of water through a membrane from a weaker solution to a stronger one.
items.example_sentence: Plant roots take in water by osmosis.

items.title: Science word: hypothesis
items.body: Meaning: a proposed explanation that can be tested by experiment or observation.
items.example_sentence: Her hypothesis was that plants grow faster with music.

items.title: Light versus sound
items.body: Physics check.
items.statement: Sound travels faster than light
items.explanation: Light moves at about 300,000 km per second; sound in air at about 0.34 km per second. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

items.title: Counting bones
items.body: Human body check.
items.statement: An adult human usually has 206 bones
items.explanation: Adults usually have 206 bones. Babies have more, around 270, and many fuse as they grow.

items.title: Antibiotics and colds
items.body: Health check.
items.statement: Antibiotics cure viral infections like the common cold
items.explanation: Colds and flu are caused by viruses. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, and misusing them causes resistance.

items.title: Our Sun
items.body: Space check.
items.statement: The Sun is a star
items.explanation: The Sun is a medium-sized star, a huge ball of hot gas powered by nuclear fusion.

items.title: Cooking on a mountain
items.body: Physics check.
items.statement: Water boils at a lower temperature high on a mountain
items.explanation: Lower air pressure at altitude lowers the boiling point. On Everest water boils at about 70 °C.

items.title: Hottest planet check
items.body: Space check.
items.statement: Mercury is the hottest planet in our solar system
items.explanation: Venus is hotter (about 465 °C) because its thick atmosphere traps heat, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

items.title: What diamonds are made of
items.body: Chemistry check.
items.statement: Diamonds are made of carbon
items.explanation: Diamond is pure carbon with its atoms locked in a very strong 3D pattern.

items.title: The main gas in air
items.body: Earth science check.
items.statement: Oxygen is the most common gas in Earth's air
items.explanation: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

items.title: Are bats birds?
items.body: Biology check.
items.statement: Bats are mammals
items.explanation: Bats have fur, give birth to live young and feed them milk. They are the only mammals capable of true flight.

items.title: Lightning myths
items.body: Weather check.
items.statement: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
items.explanation: Tall structures are hit again and again. New York's Empire State Building is struck many times every year.

items.title: E = mc²
items.body: Mass and energy are interchangeable, and c² is enormous. Converting 1 gram of mass entirely into energy would release about 90 trillion joules, roughly a 20-kiloton explosion. Nuclear fission converts only about 0.1% of the fuel's mass, yet beats coal millions of times over.

items.title: Relativity keeps GPS accurate
items.body: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day on ground clocks: weaker gravity speeds them up (general relativity) more than their speed slows them (special relativity). Uncorrected, positions would drift by around 10 km a day.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Error analysis for the Global Positioning System

items.title: Entropy and the second law
items.body: In an isolated system, entropy (disorder) never decreases. Heat flows from hot to cold on its own, and no engine can turn heat entirely into work. This law sets the maximum efficiency of every power station and car engine.

items.title: Maxwell's equations
items.body: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell summed up electricity and magnetism in a few equations and predicted waves travelling at the speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave. Radio, radar, Wi-Fi and mobile networks all follow from his work.

items.title: Quantum tunnelling
items.body: Quantum particles can cross barriers they could never climb classically. Flash memory in phones and USB sticks stores data by tunnelling electrons through a thin insulating layer, and tunnelling lets fusion happen inside the Sun.

items.title: Why semiconductors work
items.body: Silicon has a small band gap, so a few electrons can jump into the conduction band at room temperature. Adding tiny amounts of phosphorus (n-type) or boron (p-type) controls its conductivity precisely: the basis of diodes, transistors and solar cells.

items.title: Radiocarbon dating
items.body: Living things absorb carbon-14; after death it decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years. Measuring what remains dates bones, wood and cloth up to about 50,000 years old.

items.title: The Doppler effect
items.body: A wave's frequency shifts when its source moves: a siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it leaves. Police speed radar, weather radar, ultrasound blood-flow scans and measurements of the expanding universe all use it.

items.title: CRISPR gene editing
items.body: CRISPR-Cas9, adapted from a bacterial immune system, cuts DNA at a chosen spot so genes can be edited. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, and in 2023 the first CRISPR therapy was approved, for sickle cell disease.

items.title: Electrons in a wire
items.body: Physics check.
items.statement: Electrons in a copper wire travel at close to the speed of light
items.explanation: The electrical signal travels at a large fraction of light speed, but each electron drifts at well under a millimetre per second.

items.title: Which way heat flows
items.body: Thermodynamics check.
items.statement: Heat flows from a cold object to a hot one by itself
items.explanation: By the second law, heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold. Moving it the other way, as a fridge does, needs work.

items.title: Everything is binary
items.body: Computers store everything as bits, 0 or 1, because a transistor is easiest to use as an on/off switch. 8 bits make a byte with 256 possible values. Text, photos, music and apps are all just long patterns of bits with agreed meanings.

items.title: Moore's law
items.body: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly; he later settled on about every two years. That steady doubling drove 50 years of cheaper, faster computers. It has slowed as transistors approach the size of a few atoms.

items.title: Billions of switches in your pocket
items.body: A modern flagship phone processor contains around 15 to 20 billion transistors, each a tiny switch only a few tens of atoms across in places. The first commercial microprocessor, Intel's 4004 from 1971, had about 2,300.

items.title: RAM versus storage
items.body: RAM is the fast working memory where running apps live; it forgets everything when power goes off. Storage (flash or SSD) is slower but keeps data. A phone with little RAM closes background apps often; one with little storage runs out of room for photos.

items.title: What an operating system does
items.body: The operating system (Android, iOS, Windows, Linux) shares the hardware between apps. It schedules which program uses the CPU, gives each app its own protected memory, manages files, and controls access to the camera, network and sensors through permissions.

items.title: Compilers and interpreters
items.body: CPUs only run machine code. A compiler translates a whole program (C, Rust, Dart) into machine code before it runs, which makes it fast. An interpreter translates and runs code line by line (classic Python), which is flexible but slower. Many languages mix both with just-in-time compilation.

items.title: Big-O notation
items.body: Big-O describes how an algorithm's work grows with input size n. O(1) is constant, O(log n) grows very slowly, O(n) grows in step, O(n²) explodes: ten times more data means a hundred times more work. Choosing a better algorithm often beats buying a faster computer.

items.title: Binary search
items.body: To find a name in a sorted list, check the middle, then throw away the half it cannot be in, and repeat. Each step halves the list, so a million sorted items need at most about 20 checks. That is O(log n), versus up to a million checks looking one by one.

items.title: IPv4 ran out, so IPv6 arrived
items.body: Every device online needs an IP address. IPv4 uses 32 bits, about 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out as phones spread. IPv6 uses 128 bits, enough for about 3.4 × 10^38 addresses. Meanwhile routers share one public IPv4 address between many devices using NAT.

items.title: DNS: the internet's phone book
items.body: Computers route traffic by IP address, but people remember names. The Domain Name System turns a name like wikipedia.org into an IP address, using a worldwide hierarchy of servers and caching answers so repeat lookups are fast. If DNS fails, sites look 'down' even when they are not.

items.title: What the padlock means
items.body: HTTPS encrypts traffic between your browser and the site, and a certificate proves you are talking to the real domain. It stops people on the same Wi-Fi reading or changing your data. It does not prove the site is honest: scam sites can have padlocks too.

items.title: Public-key cryptography
items.body: Each person has a key pair. Anything locked with your public key can only be unlocked with your private key, so strangers can send you secrets without meeting first. Reversed, it makes digital signatures: only your private key can produce a signature your public key verifies.

items.title: Why sites store password hashes
items.body: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed. Good sites store a salted, slow hash of your password, not the password. If the database leaks, attackers must guess passwords one by one, which is why long unique passwords matter.

items.title: Phishing
items.body: Phishing tricks you into giving away passwords, codes or money with a message that looks official: a bank, a delivery, a mobile money 'reversal'. Warning signs: urgency, odd links, requests for PINs or one-time codes. Real banks and mobile money providers never ask for your PIN.

items.title: Two-factor authentication
items.body: 2FA asks for something you know (password) plus something you have (a code from an app or a security key). A stolen password alone is then not enough. Authenticator apps are safer than SMS codes, because SIM-swap fraud can redirect your texts.

items.title: Machine learning in one idea
items.body: Instead of writing rules by hand, you show a model many examples and let it adjust its internal numbers until its answers match. Spam filters, face unlock, crop disease detection and speech recognition all learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules.

items.title: How large language models work
items.body: A large language model is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token (a word piece). Doing that well forces it to learn grammar, facts and reasoning patterns. It can still state false things confidently, so check important answers.

items.title: Why GPUs power AI
items.body: A CPU has a few powerful cores; a GPU has thousands of simpler ones built to do the same maths on lots of numbers at once. Training neural networks is mostly multiplying huge matrices, exactly the parallel work GPUs were designed for when drawing game graphics.

items.title: Cloud computing
items.body: The cloud is other people's computers in data centres, rented by the hour. Startups can launch without buying servers and scale up when users arrive. The trade-offs: ongoing costs, dependence on a provider, and needing a good internet connection.

items.title: The internet runs under the sea
items.body: Almost all data travelling between continents goes through fibre-optic cables on the ocean floor, not satellites. Hundreds of these cables link the world, and damage to a few, as happened off West Africa in 2024, can slow internet access across many countries.

items.title: Mobile money changed Africa
items.body: Kenya's M-Pesa, launched in 2007, let people send money by SMS with no bank account. Zimbabwe's EcoCash followed in 2011. Mobile money spread fastest in Africa because phones reached people long before bank branches did.

items.title: Open-source software
items.body: Open-source code can be read, changed and shared by anyone. Linux runs most web servers and sits at the heart of Android. Companies use and contribute to open source because shared foundations are cheaper and better tested than everyone building their own.

items.title: Git and version control
items.body: Git, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, records every change to a project's files. You can see who changed what, undo mistakes, and let many people work in parallel on branches, then merge. Almost all professional software is built this way.

items.title: APIs: how apps talk
items.body: An API is a published set of requests one program can make to another. A weather app asks a weather service's API for today's forecast; a shop checkout calls a payment API. APIs let companies build on each other without sharing their internal code.

items.title: Latency versus bandwidth
items.body: Bandwidth is how much data per second a link carries (a wide pipe). Latency is how long one message takes to arrive (a long pipe). Streaming video needs bandwidth; video calls and online games need low latency. Satellites in high orbit add big delays.

items.title: Quantum computers
items.body: Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in combinations of 0 and 1 and become entangled. They are not faster at everything, but some problems, such as simulating molecules or factoring big numbers with Shor's algorithm, could become practical. That second one threatens today's RSA encryption.

items.title: Who makes the world's chips
items.body: Designing a chip and making it are different businesses. Apple, Nvidia and Qualcomm design chips; Taiwan's TSMC manufactures most of the world's most advanced ones. A modern chip factory costs over 20 billion US dollars, which is why so few companies can build them.

items.title: Bits and bytes
items.body: Computing check.
items.statement: A byte is made of 8 bits
items.explanation: A byte is 8 bits, giving 2^8 = 256 possible values, enough for one character of basic text.

items.title: Reading binary
items.body: Number systems check.
items.statement: 1010 in binary equals 10 in decimal

items.title: Reading hexadecimal
items.body: Number systems check.
items.statement: FF in hexadecimal equals 255 in decimal
items.explanation: F is 15, so FF = 15×16 + 15 = 255, the largest value one byte can hold.

items.title: Wi-Fi and the internet
items.body: Networking check.
items.statement: Wi-Fi and the internet are the same thing
items.correct_answer: Wi-Fi is only the local wireless link
items.explanation: Wi-Fi connects your device to a nearby router. The router then connects to the internet through your provider.

items.title: Speed of binary search
items.body: Algorithms check.
items.statement: Binary search on a sorted list takes O(n) steps
items.explanation: Each step halves the list, so the number of steps grows with log n, not n.

items.title: Incognito mode
items.body: Privacy check.
items.statement: Incognito mode hides your browsing from your internet provider
items.correct_answer: It only stops your own device keeping history
items.explanation: Private browsing does not save history or cookies on your device. Your provider, school or employer can still see which sites you reach.

chapters.title: Startups: from idea to product
chapters.summary: What makes a startup different from a small business, finding a real problem, the lean startup loop, MVPs, product-market fit, pivots and the metrics that matter early.
chapters.body:
## A startup is built to grow

Every startup is a new business, but not every new business is a startup. A barbershop or a hardware shop can be an excellent business that grows steadily. A **startup** is designed to search for a business model that can grow **very fast**, usually by using technology so that serving the next thousand customers costs little extra.

That goal changes everything: how you fund it, who you hire, and how much risk you take. Most startups fail. The ones that succeed can become enormous: Stripe, Airbnb, Flutterwave.

## Start with a painful problem

The most common reason startups fail is building something nobody wants. So start with a **problem**, not a product:

- **Who** has the problem? Be specific: "small shop owners in Harare who sell on credit", not "everyone".
- **How painful** is it? Are they already spending time or money on a bad solution? That is the strongest signal.
- **Why now?** What has changed, such as cheaper smartphones, mobile money or new regulations, that makes a solution possible today?

Talk to potential customers before you build. Ask about their past behaviour ("How did you handle this last month?"), not hypothetical opinions ("Would you use an app that...?"). People are polite about ideas; their actions tell the truth.

## The lean startup

Eric Ries's book *The Lean Startup* (2011) popularised a method borrowed from science and from lean manufacturing. Treat your business plan as a set of **hypotheses**, and test them quickly:

- **Build** the smallest thing that tests your riskiest assumption.
- **Measure** what real users actually do.
- **Learn** whether the hypothesis was right.

Then decide to **persevere** or **pivot**. The aim is to learn as much as possible for as little time and money as possible, because a startup's real enemy is running out of runway before finding something that works.

![Each turn of the loop tests an idea with a small product and real data, then you persevere or pivot.](lean_loop)

## The minimum viable product

A **minimum viable product (MVP)** is the simplest version of the product that lets you learn. It can be surprisingly basic:

- A landing page describing the product, measuring how many people sign up.
- A **concierge MVP**: you do the service by hand, such as matching customers to plumbers over WhatsApp, before writing any code.
- A **Wizard of Oz MVP**: it looks automated to the user, but people do the work behind the scenes.

Dropbox famously tested demand with a short demo video before the product was finished; sign-ups for its waiting list jumped overnight. If you're not a little embarrassed by your first version, you probably launched too late.

## Product-market fit

**Product-market fit** means you have built something a clear market strongly wants. Before it, everything feels like pushing a boulder uphill. After it, customers pull the product out of your hands: usage grows by word of mouth, and people are upset when it's down.

Signals to watch:

- **Retention:** do users keep coming back weeks later? A flattening retention curve (a stable group that stays) is the single best sign.
- **Organic growth:** do new users arrive through referrals without paid advertising?
- **Willingness to pay**, and customers asking for more.

Before product-market fit, focus almost entirely on the product and a small group of users. After it, focus shifts to scaling: hiring, sales and raising money.

## Pivots

A **pivot** is a change in one fundamental part of the strategy while keeping what you have learned. Famous pivots:

- **Slack** began as an internal chat tool inside a company building an online game called *Glitch*. The game failed; the chat tool became Slack.
- **Instagram** started as *Burbn*, a check-in app with many features. The founders noticed people mainly used photo sharing and cut everything else.

A pivot is not failure; it is the lean loop working. But pivoting every month without learning anything is just thrashing.

## The founding team

Investors often say they back teams before ideas, because ideas change and teams execute. Strong founding teams:

- combine skills, typically someone who **builds** (technical) and someone who **sells**;
- have worked together before or know each other well;
- agree early and in writing on roles, ownership and **vesting**.

## Startups in Africa

African startups often solve problems that were solved long ago elsewhere: payments, logistics, credit, energy, health access. Mobile phones reached people before banks, roads and power grids did, which is why mobile money, pay-as-you-go solar and mobile health spread so quickly. Designing for low data costs, unreliable power, feature phones and cash-heavy customers is a real advantage for local founders.
key_points: A startup is a business designed to grow very fast, usually using technology.
Start with a painful, specific problem, and learn from customers' past behaviour, not opinions.
The lean startup loop: build the smallest test, measure real behaviour, learn, then persevere or pivot.
An MVP exists to learn; it can be a landing page or a manual service.
Retention is the best early signal of product-market fit.
Pivots such as Slack and Instagram change strategy while keeping what was learned.

quiz.question: What most distinguishes a startup from other small businesses?
options: It is designed to find a business model that can grow very fast
quiz.explanation: Startups aim for rapid, scalable growth, which shapes their funding and risk-taking.

quiz.question: Which customer interview question gives the most reliable information?
options: "Would you use an app that solves this?"
"How did you handle this problem last month?"
"How much would you pay in future?"
quiz.explanation: Past behaviour is evidence; opinions about hypothetical products are often just politeness.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of an MVP?
options: To impress investors with a finished product
To learn whether customers want the product with minimum effort
quiz.explanation: An MVP tests the riskiest assumption as cheaply as possible.

quiz.question: Which metric is the strongest early sign of product-market fit?
options: Retention: users continuing to come back over time
quiz.explanation: Downloads can be bought; users who keep returning show real value.

quiz.explanation: The game Glitch failed, but its team's internal chat tool became Slack.

chapters.title: Venture capital: how startups raise money
chapters.summary: How VC funds work and why they chase huge outcomes, funding rounds, valuation and dilution, SAFEs, the term sheet clauses that matter, and alternatives to VC.
chapters.body:
## Where VC money comes from

A **venture capital (VC) fund** is a pool of money managed by a VC firm. The firm's partners, the **general partners (GPs)**, choose the investments. The money mostly comes from **limited partners (LPs)**: pension funds, university endowments, insurance companies, development finance institutions and wealthy families.

A typical fund lasts about **ten years**: it invests in its first few years, helps companies grow, then returns money to LPs as companies are sold or listed. GPs are commonly paid "**2 and 20**": an annual management fee of about 2% of the fund, plus about 20% of the profits (**carried interest**).

## The power law

Most startups fail, and many of the rest return little. VC returns follow a **power law**: one outstanding company often returns more than all the others combined. So a VC must ask of every investment: **could this return the entire fund?**

This explains VC behaviour that otherwise seems strange. VCs prefer huge markets, accept high risk, push for fast growth, and pass on good businesses that are unlikely to become very large. A company that grows steadily into a profitable 5-million-dollar business can be a great outcome for its founders and a poor one for a VC fund.

## Funding rounds

Startups raise money in stages, each meant to reach milestones that justify a higher valuation next time:

- **Pre-seed:** founders, friends and family, angels and accelerators. Money to build the first version.
- **Seed:** angels and seed funds. Money to find product-market fit.
- **Series A:** the first big institutional round, for a company with clear traction that needs to scale.
- **Series B, C and later:** larger rounds to expand into new markets, products and teams.
- **Exit:** investors get their return when the company is **acquired** or lists on a stock exchange in an **initial public offering (IPO)**.

![Each round sells part of the company at a higher valuation; founders own a smaller share of something more valuable.](funding_stages)

## Valuation and dilution

When an investor buys new shares, the key numbers are:

- **Pre-money valuation:** what the company is agreed to be worth before the new money.
- **Post-money valuation** = pre-money + new investment.
- **Investor's ownership** = investment ÷ post-money.

> Worked example: an investor puts in 2 million at an 8 million pre-money valuation. Post-money = 10 million, so the investor owns 2 ÷ 10 = 20%. A founder who owned 50% before now owns 50% × 0.8 = 40%.

That drop is **dilution**. It is not bad in itself. Right after the round, the founder's stake is worth the same on paper: 50% of 8 million and 40% of 10 million are both 4 million. Dilution pays off when the cash grows the company's value faster than your percentage shrinks: if the company later reaches 50 million, that 40% is worth 20 million. Founders track all of this in a **cap table**, a spreadsheet showing who owns what.

Companies also set aside an **option pool**, typically 10–20% of shares, to attract employees with stock options. Investors often require the pool to be created before their investment, so it dilutes only the founders.

## SAFEs and convertible notes

Agreeing a valuation for a very young company is hard, so early rounds often use instruments that convert into shares later:

- A **SAFE** (simple agreement for future equity), created by Y Combinator in 2013, gives the investor the right to shares in a future priced round. It usually has a **valuation cap** (a maximum valuation at which it converts) and sometimes a **discount**.
- A **convertible note** is similar but is technically a loan, with interest and a maturity date.

They are fast and cheap to arrange, but stacking many of them can cause surprise dilution when they all convert.

## The term sheet

A **term sheet** summarises the deal. Beyond valuation, founders should understand:

- **Liquidation preference:** in a sale, investors get their money back (usually 1×) before common shareholders. **Participating** preferences let them take their money back *and* share in the rest, which is much worse for founders.
- **Board composition:** who controls the board controls the company, including hiring and firing the CEO.
- **Protective provisions:** investor vetoes over major decisions such as new share issues or selling the company.
- **Pro-rata rights:** the right to invest in future rounds to keep their percentage.
- **Anti-dilution protection:** adjusts investor shares if a later round is priced lower (a **down round**).

A founder who focuses only on the highest valuation can end up with harsh terms that matter far more.

## Alternatives to venture capital

VC suits only a small fraction of businesses. Alternatives include:

- **Bootstrapping** from revenue, keeping full control.
- **Angel investors**, often more flexible than funds.
- **Grants and competitions**, common for African startups from foundations and development agencies.
- **Revenue-based financing**, repaid as a percentage of revenue.
- **Bank loans and asset finance**, for businesses with steady cash flow and collateral.

## The African picture

Venture investment in Africa grew rapidly from the mid-2010s, peaked in 2021–2022, then fell back as global interest rates rose. Most of the money has gone to fintech and to four markets: Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Egypt. Founders elsewhere, including in Zimbabwe, often incorporate a holding company abroad, commonly in Delaware or Mauritius, because many investors prefer familiar legal systems. Get legal and tax advice before doing this.
key_points: VC funds invest LPs' money, last about ten years, and are paid through fees and carried interest.
Returns follow a power law, so VCs back companies that could return the whole fund.
Post-money = pre-money + investment; investor ownership = investment ÷ post-money.
Dilution is worthwhile only if the money grows the company's value faster.
SAFEs and convertible notes delay valuation; watch valuation caps and stacked dilution.
Liquidation preferences and board control can matter more than the headline valuation.

quiz.question: An investor puts 1 million into a startup at a 3 million pre-money valuation. What percentage do they own afterwards?
quiz.explanation: Post-money = 3 + 1 = 4 million, so ownership = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

quiz.question: Why do VCs pass on some good, profitable businesses?
options: Their returns depend on a few huge winners, so they need companies that could return the whole fund
They only invest in loss-making companies
They are legally barred from profitable companies
They only invest in public companies
quiz.explanation: The power law means only very large outcomes move a VC fund's returns.

quiz.question: What does a 1× non-participating liquidation preference mean when a company is sold?
options: Investors get nothing until founders are paid
Investors can take their money back first, before common shareholders
quiz.explanation: Preferred investors can recover their investment first, or convert to common shares if that pays more.

quiz.question: What is a SAFE?
options: An agreement giving the investor shares in a future priced round
A type of stock exchange listing
quiz.explanation: Created by Y Combinator in 2013, a SAFE converts into equity later, often subject to a valuation cap.

quiz.question: Who are a VC fund's limited partners?
options: Institutions and wealthy investors who supply most of the fund's money
quiz.explanation: LPs such as pension funds and endowments provide capital; GPs manage the fund.

chapters.title: The numbers: margins, unit economics and runway
chapters.summary: Revenue, costs and gross margin, break-even, customer acquisition cost and lifetime value, churn, burn rate and runway, and the three financial statements.
chapters.body:
## Why founders must know the numbers

A great product can still sink a company if every sale loses money or the bank account runs dry. You do not need to be an accountant, but you must understand a handful of numbers well enough to spot danger early. Investors will ask about them in the first meeting.

## Revenue, costs and gross margin

- **Revenue** is the money earned from sales.
- **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** is the direct cost of delivering what you sold: materials, hosting per user, payment fees, delivery.
- **Gross profit** = revenue − COGS.
- **Gross margin** = gross profit ÷ revenue.

> Example: a solar lamp sells for 40 and costs 28 to make, ship and collect payment for. Gross profit = 12, gross margin = 12 ÷ 40 = 30%.

Gross margin shows how much of each sale is left to pay for everything else. Software often has margins above 70%, because another copy costs almost nothing. Hardware, retail and logistics businesses are often at 20–40%, so they need much larger volumes.

## Fixed costs, variable costs and break-even

**Variable costs** rise with each unit sold (materials, delivery). **Fixed costs** stay the same regardless of sales (rent, salaries, software subscriptions).

The **break-even point** is where total profit is zero:

> Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit)

If fixed costs are 6,000 a month and each lamp earns 12 after variable costs, you must sell 6,000 ÷ 12 = 500 lamps a month to break even. Every lamp after that adds 12 of profit. This is **operating leverage**: once fixed costs are covered, profits grow quickly.

## Unit economics: CAC and LTV

**Unit economics** asks whether a single customer is profitable.

- **Customer acquisition cost (CAC)** = total sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers won. If you spend 3,000 on ads and agents and win 100 customers, CAC = 30.
- **Lifetime value (LTV)** is the gross profit a customer brings over their whole relationship with you. For a subscription: LTV ≈ monthly gross profit per customer ÷ monthly churn rate.
- **Churn** is the share of customers who leave each period. A monthly churn of 5% means the average customer stays about 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months.

> Example: a customer pays 10 a month at 70% gross margin (7 gross profit), and monthly churn is 5%. LTV ≈ 7 ÷ 0.05 = 140. With CAC = 30, LTV ÷ CAC ≈ 4.7.

A common rule of thumb is **LTV at least 3 × CAC**, with CAC recovered within about 12 months (the **payback period**). If LTV is below CAC, growing faster just loses money faster.

## Burn rate and runway

- **Gross burn** is total monthly spending; **net burn** is spending minus revenue, the cash you actually lose each month.
- **Runway** = cash in the bank ÷ net burn.

With 600,000 in the bank and a net burn of 50,000 a month, runway is 12 months. Raising money typically takes three to six months, so founders start fundraising with plenty of runway left. Paul Graham calls a startup **default alive** if, at current growth and costs, it will reach profitability before its cash runs out, and **default dead** if it won't.

![The same 600k lasts exactly 12 months at a flat 50k burn, but growing revenue can turn the curve before the cash runs out.](runway_chart)

## The three financial statements

Every company produces three core reports:

- **Income statement** (profit and loss): revenue minus expenses over a period gives **net profit**.
- **Balance sheet**: a snapshot of what the company owns (**assets**) and owes (**liabilities**) at one moment. The difference is **equity**: assets = liabilities + equity.
- **Cash flow statement**: actual cash moving in and out, from operations, investing and financing.

They tell different stories. A company can be **profitable but out of cash** if customers pay in 90 days while suppliers must be paid in 30, or if it buys lots of stock. Many businesses that fail were profitable on paper. Watch **cash flow** weekly, chase unpaid invoices, and negotiate payment terms.

## Metrics that can fool you

- **Vanity metrics:** total downloads and registered users always go up and hide whether people stay. Prefer active users and retention.
- **Revenue growth bought with discounts:** if customers leave when prices return to normal, you bought revenue, not demand.
- **Averages that hide cohorts:** look at each month's new customers (a **cohort**) separately to see whether retention is improving.

## Pricing is a lever

Raising prices by 10% with the same costs flows almost entirely to profit, while cutting costs by 10% is usually much harder. Price according to the **value** customers receive, not just your costs. Test prices, and remember that the right customers often care more about reliability than a small discount.
key_points: Gross margin = (revenue − COGS) ÷ revenue; it shows what each sale leaves to cover other costs.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit).
CAC is the cost to win a customer; LTV is the gross profit they bring; aim for LTV ≥ 3 × CAC.
Runway = cash ÷ net burn; start fundraising well before it runs out.
Profit is not cash: the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement tell different stories.
Beware vanity metrics; track retention by cohort.

quiz.question: A product sells for 50 and costs 35 to produce and deliver. What is its gross margin?
quiz.explanation: Gross profit is 15, and 15 ÷ 50 = 30%.

quiz.question: Fixed costs are 8,000 a month; price is 20 and variable cost is 12 per unit. What is the break-even volume?
quiz.explanation: Each unit contributes 20 − 12 = 8, and 8,000 ÷ 8 = 1,000 units.

quiz.question: A startup has 300,000 in cash and a net burn of 25,000 a month. What is its runway?
How can a profitable company run out of cash?
options: It cannot; profit always means cash
Customers pay slowly while costs and suppliers must be paid now
Profit is only calculated once a year
The balance sheet is always wrong
quiz.explanation: Timing differences between earning revenue and receiving cash can empty the bank account.

quiz.question: Monthly gross profit per customer is 6 and monthly churn is 3%. Roughly what is the LTV?

chapters.title: Strategy: competition, moats and growth
chapters.summary: Porter's five forces, cost leadership versus differentiation, the moats that protect profits, network effects, go-to-market choices and tools like SWOT and the business model canvas.
chapters.body:
## What strategy is

Strategy is the set of choices about **where to compete** and **how to win**, and just as importantly, what **not** to do. A strategy that tries to serve everyone with everything is not a strategy. Good strategy explains why customers will choose you over the alternatives, and why competitors can't simply copy you.

## Porter's five forces

In 1979, Harvard professor Michael Porter described five forces that decide how profitable an industry is:

- **Rivalry among existing competitors.** Many similar firms fighting on price destroy profits.
- **Threat of new entrants.** If starting up is cheap and easy, profits attract newcomers until they disappear.
- **Threat of substitutes.** Different products solving the same need: mobile money is a substitute for bank transfers, and video calls for business flights.
- **Bargaining power of suppliers.** A sole supplier of a key component can raise prices and take your margin.
- **Bargaining power of buyers.** Large customers, or customers who can switch easily, push prices down.

![The five forces: rivalry at the centre, pressed by new entrants, substitutes, suppliers and buyers.](five_forces)

Airlines face all five strongly and have historically struggled to make money. Software platforms with loyal users face weak forces and earn high margins. Before entering a market, ask which forces will squeeze you.

## Generic strategies

Porter also argued that firms win in one of a few basic ways:

- **Cost leadership:** be the cheapest producer, through scale, efficiency or a simpler product, and win on price.
- **Differentiation:** offer something customers value and will pay more for: quality, brand, design, service or features.
- **Focus:** apply either approach to a narrow segment, such as a specific region or customer type, better than broad competitors can.

The danger is being "**stuck in the middle**": neither cheapest nor clearly better.

## Moats

A **moat**, a term popularised by investor Warren Buffett, is a durable advantage that protects profits from competitors:

- **Network effects:** the product becomes more valuable as more people use it.
- **Switching costs:** leaving is painful because of data, integrations, retraining or contracts. Accounting software and banking relationships are examples.
- **Economies of scale:** unit costs fall with size, so big players can undercut newcomers.
- **Brand:** trust and recognition that let you charge more.
- **Intangible assets:** patents, licences and regulatory approvals.
- **Proprietary data or technology** that others can't easily replicate.

Startups rarely begin with a moat. They usually win at first through speed and focus, then build moats as they grow.

## Network effects in detail

With **direct** network effects, each new user adds value for every other user: WhatsApp is useless if none of your contacts use it. **Two-sided** (indirect) network effects link different groups: more riders attract more drivers on a ride-hailing app, which cuts waiting times and attracts more riders.

Mobile money is a powerful example. Each new EcoCash or M-Pesa user makes the network more useful for everyone they might pay, and more merchants accept it, which attracts more users. Network effects make markets tend towards one or two winners, which is why startups in these markets fight hard for early growth, and why regulators worry about dominance.

The hard part is the **cold start**: the first users get little value. Common tactics are to start in a small, dense community (one campus or one market), subsidise one side, or offer a useful single-player tool first.

## Go-to-market

How will customers find and buy your product?

- **Product-led growth:** users try it free and upgrade; it works best for simple, low-cost products.
- **Sales-led:** a sales team sells to businesses; it suits complex or expensive products.
- **Agent networks:** common in Africa for mobile money, insurance and solar, where trust and cash handling need a local person.
- **Partnerships:** distributing through a bank, telecom or retailer that already has the customers.

The best channel matches your price: a product earning 5 dollars a year can't afford a salesperson for each customer.

## Two quick planning tools
